title: Classic car restoration in Rioz: how the SAVA workshop actually works
author: codex-blog-rewrite
excerpt: In Rioz, SAVA approaches the restoration of an older car through concrete stages: inspection, dismantling, mechanical work, trim, finishes and careful reassembly.
content:
In Rioz, SAVA does not use “classic car restoration” as a vague label. On the page dedicated to older cars, the workshop points to very concrete areas instead: engine, chassis, running gear, braking, upholstery, treated fasteners and blasted, protected parts. A full restoration therefore means much more than a fresh coat of paint or a car that looks better in photographs. It begins with the real state of the vehicle, then moves through a sequence of technical choices that have to remain coherent all the way to final reassembly.

That method is visible in the cars already shown by SAVA: 2CV, Simca Aronde A90, Mazda 818 coupé from 1977, Mazda 929 and Mazda RX-7. The models change, the parts do not age in the same way, yet the principle stays stable. First, the workshop has to see what can honestly be kept, what has to be corrected without delay and what is worth rebuilding while the car is apart.

Starting from the actual car, not from the final image

With an old car, there is always a temptation to think backwards: picture the finished vehicle before accepting the starting point. The Rioz workshop works the other way around. The first task is to look at the structure, the safety organs, the corrosion points and the inconsistencies left by earlier work. That step takes time, but it prevents a neat rebuild from being placed on a base that was never properly understood.

In practice, this means opening, removing, cleaning, checking and then ranking the priorities. A tired running gear is not limited to another invoice line. A doubtful braking system, a badly repaired shell or a mechanical unit that has stood still for a long time changes the whole method of the project. At that stage, real skill is not a matter of language. It lies in being able to read the car for what it still is, not just for what one hopes it will become again.

A full restoration always combines several trades

That is also what makes the SAVA page useful: restoration is not split into isolated boxes. Heavy mechanical work is not separated from trim, and fastener treatment is not disconnected from finishing work. On an older car, those areas constantly interact. A clean reassembly depends on sound parts, hardware that will last, an interior that matches the intended use and components brought back into condition before the shell is closed again.

A 2CV is a good example. The project cannot be judged only by the final silhouette, but by the quality of the underbody, the seriousness of the restart, the choice of wear parts and the way the whole car is put back together. A Simca Aronde or a late-1970s Mazda requires different decisions afterwards, yet the same discipline underneath. That is why a completed restoration always takes longer than a simple cosmetic refresh.

Rioz: a workshop where restoration stays tangible

What finally comes through in SAVA’s work is a scale that still feels readable. This is not an abstract display of “premium services”, but a workshop that shows precise cases, real interventions and cars that actually passed through its hands. That measure matters. It says more about the rhythm, care and limits of a restoration project than a smoother sales pitch ever could.

To place the workshop itself in context, the page SAVA in Rioz gives the overall frame. And when the project also demands deeper work inside the cabin, the article on automotive upholstery at SAVA is the natural next step.
